content.text:
Such problems and solutions were well understood in ancient India. In fact, a very systematic way to solve problems with single unknowns was first proposed by Aryabhata (499 CE) and Brahmagupta has outlined it in his Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta (628 CE). Let us understand his method.
Let us look at a few equations of the following form: 5x + 4 = 3x + 8, or 3x − 6 = 2x + 4.
Can we come up with a formula to solve these equations? That is, for the first equation, can we perform some operations using 5, 4, 3, and 8 that will directly give us the solution? Using a similar method, can you solve the second equation using the numbers 3, −6, 2 and 4?
To get a formula, we can generalise equations of this form by taking the four numbers as A, B, C, and D. That is, Ax + B = Cx + D.
Brahmagupta gives the solution to equations of this form with this formula: x = (D − B)/(A − C).
Using this approach, we can find the solution to the equation 650m + 4000 = 500m + 5050 simply by calculating m = (5050 − 4000)/(650 − 500).
Using this formula can you solve this equation 2x + 3 = 4x + 5?
Ancient Indian mathematicians were excellent at converting complex mathematical ideas into simple procedures so that everyone could use these procedures to solve problems!
Bījagaṇita or algebra is the branch of mathematics that uses letter symbols to solve mathematical problems. We have seen some examples in previous pages. By studying algebra, we learn to generalise patterns, in numbers, shapes, and situations. We express these generalisations using the language of algebra, which is both precise and powerful. Bījagaṇita also gives us a way to justify mathematical claims (like why the sum of two odd numbers is always even) and to solve problems of many kinds.
The power of algebra was well recognised by ancient Indian mathematicians. We hope you recognise it too, and enjoy using it!

content.text:
Solve Ax + B = Cx + D with letters instead of numbers: move Cx to the left and B to the right.
Ax − Cx = D − B, so (A − C)x = D − B.
Divide both sides by A − C: x = (D − B)/(A − C), when A and C are different.
The rule is the balance moves done once, for every equation of this shape.

content.text:
Use Brahmagupta's rule to solve 650m + 4000 = 500m + 5050.
1. Match the shape Ax + B = Cx + D: A = 650, B = 4000, C = 500, D = 5050.
2. m = (D − B)/(A − C) = (5050 − 4000)/(650 − 500).
3. 5050 − 4000 = 1050 and 650 − 500 = 150.
4. m = 1050 ÷ 150 = 7, the same as in Jahnavi and Sunita's savings.
Answer: m = 7

content.text: One man has ₹$300$ and $6$ horses. Another has $10$ horses and a debt of ₹$100$. They are equally rich, and every horse has the same price. Find the price of one horse.

content.publication_text: One man has ₹$300$ and $6$ horses. Another has $10$ horses and a debt of ₹$100$. They are equally rich, and every horse has the same price. Find the price of one horse.

content.text:
$1$. Let the price of one horse be ₹$x$.
$2$. First man: $300 + 6x$. Second man: $10x - 100$.
$3$. Set up: $300 + 6x = 10x - 100$.
$4$. Add $100$ to both sides: $400 + 6x = 10x$.
$5$. Subtract $6x$ from both sides: $400 = 4x$.
$6$. $x = 400 \div 4 = 100$.
$7$. Check: $300 + 6 \times 100 = 900$ and $10 \times 100 - 100 = 900$.
Answer: ₹$100$

media.description: A balance holds 5 sacks and 4 weights against 3 sacks and 8 weights. The hint matches each equation to Ax + B = Cx + D, with B = −6 in the second; then both equations are solved with the four numbers and checked.

video_script.anchor: Use only the four numbers: (i) 5x + 4 = 3x + 8 (ii) 3x − 6 = 2x + 4
video_script.design: One idea: the four numbers solve the equation, gap of lone numbers over gap of x numbers, signs kept. Assumes: the balance moves and the formula. Wrong idea: the slip drops the minus sign of B. Transitions: the anchor with both equations stays all video; the balance stays through the hint and part (i); one clear, of the working band, before the recap.
video_script.wrong_move: In the second equation the slip treats B as 6 and computes 4 − 6 = −2, so x = −2; putting it back gives 3 × (−2) − 6 = −12 on the left and 2 × (−2) + 4 = 0 on the right, not equal, and that answer is struck.
maths_rules: take 3x from both sides and 4 from both sides: 5x − 3x = 8 − 4, that is 2x = 4

balance picture for (i): left pan 5 sacks of the same weight x kg and 4 one-kilogram weights; right pan 3 sacks and 8 one-kilogram weights; removing 3 sacks and 4 weights from each pan leaves 2 sacks against 4 weights
(ii) 3x − 6 = 2x + 4: A = 3, B = −6, C = 2, D = 4; the minus sign belongs to the 6
video_script.payoff_line: The first equation gives x equals two

final_answer.spoken: x equals two, and x equals ten

video_script.substitution: The lone numbers' gap goes on top and the x numbers' gap goes below, and a negative number keeps its sign.

media.teaching_notes: The one idea: take away the smaller x side and the lone number once, which gives (D − B) ÷ (A − C). Watch for the slip in the second equation: with B = −6, D − B is 4 − (−6) = 10, not 4 − 6.

content.text:
$1$. Let the first person get $a$.
$2$. Second: $2a$. Third: $3 \times 2a = 6a$. Fourth: $4 \times 6a = 24a$.
$3$. Set up: $a + 2a + 6a + 24a = 132$, that is $33a = 132$.
$4$. $a = 132 \div 33 = 4$.
$5$. Check: $4 + 8 + 24 + 96 = 132$.
Answer: $4$

topics.summary: Summary and a magic trick.

content.text:
An algebraic equation is a mathematical statement that indicates the equality of two algebraic expressions.
When the same operation is performed on both sides of an equation, equality is maintained.
Finding a solution to an equation means finding the values of the unknowns in the expressions such that the LHS is equal to the RHS.
Equations can often be solved by performing the same operation on both sides so that the value of the unknown becomes evident.
A Magic Trick
Think of any number. Now multiply it by 2. Add 10. Divide by 2. Now subtract the original number you thought of. Finally, add 3. I predict that you now have 8. Am I correct?
Try the trick on your friends and family! Can you explain why the trick works? [Hint: Denote the first number thought of by x.] Can you make your own such tricks?

A Magic Trick
Think of any number. Now multiply it by 2. Add 10. Divide by 2. Now subtract the original number you thought of. Finally, add 3. I predict that you now have 8. Am I correct?
Try the trick on your friends and family! Can you explain why the trick works? [Hint: Denote the first number thought of by x.] Can you make your own such tricks?

content.text:
A Magic Trick: Think of any number. Multiply it by 2. Add 10. Divide by 2. Subtract the number you first thought of. Add 3. Why is the answer always 8? Can you make your own such trick?
1. Let the number be x.
2. Multiply by 2: 2x. Add 10: 2x + 10.
3. Divide by 2: (2x + 10) ÷ 2 = x + 5.
4. Subtract the number: x + 5 − x = 5. Add 3: 5 + 3 = 8.
5. The x is taken away, so the answer never depends on the starting number.
6. Your own trick: multiply by 3, add 12, divide by 3, subtract the number; the answer is always 4.
Answer: Always 8, because after dividing by 2 the expression is x + 5, and subtracting x leaves 5, then 5 + 3 = 8

objectives.objective_text: Students halve the total of a balanced mobile to find each side's weight, then find unknown weights such as the bud, fish, cloud and gem from the weights given on that side.
Students remove equal weights from both pans to find the sack on each scale, find unknowns on hand-held mobiles, and explain why the scale stays level.
Students level a two-pan scale by taking the same weight off both pans, predict which way it tips after a one-sided move, and find each hidden weight.
Students state the matchstick rule in words and as 2n + 1, write the equation 2n + 1 = 99 for Jasmine's question, and explain why no arrangement uses exactly 200 sticks.
Students identify the LHS and RHS of an equation, frame equations such as 2e = 6 and 5s = 21 + 2s for the mobiles and scales, and check each solution.
Students write a rule for each stick pattern, decide whether 85 or 150 sticks can make an arrangement, and frame the blob equation 3b + 4 = 25.
Students substitute values into 2n + 1 = 99 until LHS equals RHS, explain why n = 49 is the only solution, and show why trial and error struggles with 5x − 4 = 7.
Students find the value of an expression by removing a term or a factor from both sides, using inverse operations, as in the four examples with 88, 7, −67 and 8/9.
Students find the inputs of machines and fill blanks with integers by undoing each operation in reverse order, and compare that with guessing the input.
Students solve 5x − 4 = 7 and 11y + (−5) = 61 by removing the term and then the factor from both sides, and check each solution by substituting it.
Students solve 6y + 7 = 4y + 21 by first removing 4y from both sides, then finish in two steps and check that both sides equal 49.
Students solve and check five equations, including one with a bracket and one with a divisor, and frame an equation that has no solution.
Students rewrite the long solutions of 11y + (−5) = 61 and 6y + 7 = 4y + 21 in the short way, changing the sign of each term that moves across.
Students solve u/15 = 6 by multiplying the other side by the divisor, and state the three observations for moving a term, a factor and a divisor.
Students solve fifteen equations with signs, fractions and brackets by moving terms and factors across, and find the path through the equation maze.
Students write 3k + 1 = 100 for Ranjana's tiles and model Madhubanti's party in three ways, 25p + 50 = 500 among them, finding step 33 and 13 friends.
Students equate the savings expressions 4000 + 650m and 5050 + 500m to find 7 months, and write two unknowns with one letter to share 60 marbles.
Students set up and then solve equations for notes, a taxi fare, two numbers, a window grill, drinks, triangle angles, and heads and feet.
Students solve 28(x + 4) + 300 = 1000 by removing terms first, by dividing every term by 4, and by opening the bracket, reaching x = 21 each time.
Students write Riyaz's steps as x − 3, 4x − 12 and 4x − 4, solve 4x − 4 = 24 to find 7, and state a rule for any final answer.
Students set up and solve puzzles about a three-digit number, a brick, a giraffe, a quarter of a number and a number increased by 36.
Students build chains of equations with the solution y = 5, reverse each chain using inverse operations, and state every equation's solution without calculating.
Students give a real-life situation for 100x + 75 = 250, matching the fixed term, the changing term and the total to the story.
Students write equations with the solutions x = −2 and u = 6, and use 4k + 1 = 13 and 28p − 36 = 98 to find related expressions before solving.
Students test boxes 1 to 3 by substituting the final answer, name the broken move in each, and correct the solutions to x = 1, z = 1/4 and v = 5.
Students find the sign, like-term and partial-division mistakes in boxes 4 to 6, and correct the solutions to z = −3, w = 26/11 and x = −13/3.
Students mend bracket mistakes in boxes 7 to 9 and in three more solutions, deciding when a solution has no mistake at all.
Students explain the meaning of bīja and al-jabr, place Brahmagupta and Al-Khwarizmi in time, and write expressions such as 2x − 8 in the yā and rū notation.
Students model the horse problem as 300 + 6x = 10x − 100, treating the debt as a negative amount, and find the price of one horse.
Students derive x = (D − B)/(A − C) from Ax + B = Cx + D and apply it to three equations, including 2x + 3 = 4x + 5.
Students apply the rule to equations of the form Ax + B = Cx + D, test when it cannot work, and solve the Bakhśhāli sharing problem.
Students match each summary statement to an example, explain why the magic trick always gives 8, and solve a mixed set, choosing the first move for each equation.

tool_term_mover.idea: A term moves across the equals sign with its sign changed; a factor or divisor moves by dividing or multiplying the whole other side.
tool_term_mover.title: Term Mover
tool_term_mover.predict: Before dragging, tap the sign the term will have on the other side.
tool_term_mover.invariant: The solution of the equation never changes as terms and factors move across.

tool_chain_maker.idea: Starting from a solution and doing the same operation to both sides makes new equations with the same solution.
tool_chain_maker.title: Chain Maker
tool_chain_maker.predict: Before adding a link, say what the new equation's solution will be.
tool_chain_maker.invariant: Every equation in the chain is true for the starting value.

tool_pan_leveller.idea: A level scale stays level only when the same weight is added to or removed from both pans.
tool_pan_leveller.title: Pan Leveller
tool_pan_leveller.predict: Before any move, type your guess for one sack, and tap which way the beam will tip if you take a weight off one pan only.
tool_pan_leveller.invariant: The two pans weigh the same after every legal move; the beam shows it by staying level.

tool_rule_of_four.idea: For every equation Ax + B = Cx + D with A and C different, x = (D − B)/(A − C).
tool_rule_of_four.title: Rule of Four Numbers
tool_rule_of_four.predict: Before using the rule, guess whether x will be positive or negative.
tool_rule_of_four.invariant: The rule's answer and the step-by-step balance answer are always the same.

tool_trick_tracer.idea: Following a puzzle's steps with a letter gives an expression; setting it equal to the result gives the equation.
tool_trick_tracer.title: Trick Tracer
tool_trick_tracer.predict: Before tracing, guess the number from the result.
tool_trick_tracer.invariant: For any starting number, the expression and the step-by-step working give the same value.

tool_undo_machine.idea: To find an input, undo each operation of the machine in reverse order.
tool_undo_machine.title: Undo Machine
tool_undo_machine.predict: Before undoing, type a guess for the input and run it forwards to see how close it is.
tool_undo_machine.invariant: Running the found input forwards through the machine gives back the output.

tool_step_detective.idea: A broken step is a line whose solution differs from the line above it.
tool_step_detective.title: Step Detective
tool_step_detective.predict: Before testing, tap the line you think is broken, or 'no mistake'.
tool_step_detective.invariant: Every correct line has the same solution as the first line.

tool_story_to_equation.idea: A word problem is solved in two separate steps: write the equation from the story, then solve it.
tool_story_to_equation.title: Story to Equation Board
tool_story_to_equation.predict: Before writing anything, type a rough guess for the answer.
tool_story_to_equation.invariant: The equation's two sides are the same amount described two ways in the story.

tool_both_sides_stepper.idea: Each line of a solution comes from the line above by one operation done to both sides.
tool_both_sides_stepper.title: Both-Sides Stepper
tool_both_sides_stepper.predict: Before the first move, choose which should go first: a term or a factor.
tool_both_sides_stepper.invariant: Every line keeps the same solution; a balance icon beside each line stays level.

tool_stick_rule_builder.idea: A growing pattern's rule turns 'which position uses this many?' into an equation to solve.
tool_stick_rule_builder.title: Stick Rule Builder
tool_stick_rule_builder.predict: Before building, type how many sticks you think position 5 needs.
tool_stick_rule_builder.invariant: Each new position adds the same number of sticks, so the rule has the form (step) × n + start.

how_to_use.intro: The equals sign means 'the same as', not 'here comes the answer'. Every topic starts from a balance or a puzzle the student tries first, then turns what they did into a legal move on both sides, and only then names the rule. Equations are met in order of structure: one step, two steps, unknowns on both sides, brackets, then word problems set up in one step and solved in another.

points.text: Mobiles and two-pan scales come before any symbol. A scale that tips shows an unequal pair; taking the same off both pans keeps it level. When a student is stuck, they go back to the balance with the same numbers.
points.title: The balance first

points.text: A guess is written before any working. The check is always the same: put the value back and see whether the left side equals the right side.
points.title: Predict, then check

points.text: Each line of a solution comes from the line above by one operation done to BOTH sides. Every worked solution in this plan is machine-checked: each line keeps the same solution as the first.
points.title: Legal moves, one line at a time

points.text: Moving a term across the equals sign changes its sign; dividing a side divides every term on it. These two slips cause most wrong answers, and a whole topic is spent finding and mending them.
points.title: Signs and whole sides

points.text: First write the equation that models the story; then solve it. The two steps are checked separately, because most mistakes happen in the first.
points.title: Word problems in two steps

source_metadata.chapter_idea: An equation says that two expressions have the same value, like the two pans of a balanced scale. Doing the same thing to both sides keeps the balance, so we can remove what is added, undo what multiplies, and leave the unknown alone on one side. Forming an equation from a situation and solving it finds hidden numbers in patterns, prices, savings and puzzles.
source_notes: Book figures are mobiles (a bar hanging from its middle, with the total weight on top) and two-pan scales. A balanced mobile holds half the total on each side. Every count was read from 400 dpi renders: mobile 1 (16: leaf, bud, leaf against a flower), mobile 2 (24: star, fish, star against fish, submarine), mobile 3 (8: a book against two pencil boxes on a small bar), mobile 4 (18: a sun and 4 clouds against 3 lightning bolts), mobile 5 (40: a crown and 5 gems against 4 crowns), mobiles 6 to 8 held by a hand (3 bread slices against 2 eggs; 4 crosses against donut, cross, donut; a watermelon against banana, orange, banana), sack scales 1 to 4 (sack + 2 kg against 10 kg + 2 kg; 2 sacks against 10 kg, 4 kg and a sack; 5 sacks against 1 kg, 10 kg, 10 kg and 2 sacks; 90 sacks + 50 kg against 60 sacks + 500 kg).
